The Push for Private Listings Ignites a Real-Estate War
 
Plus, the skyrocketing cost of custom furniture and a blended family’s $4 million North Carolina home
 
By Kerry Barger
 
 
A Compass listing in Quincy, Mass., recently sold as a ‘coming soon’ listing, without going on the MLS. ERIC JOHNSON OF THE MISSION REALTY ADVISORS TEAM AT COMPASS
 

This is an edition of the WSJ Homes newsletter, a weekly guide to luxurious properties, celebrity homes, interior design and the housing market. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

Private listings. Private exclusives. “Coming soons.” Compass, now America’s largest real-estate brokerage, has changed the game by offering sellers the option to market their homes on its website before listing them on public portals like Zillow or local multiple listing services.

 

The brokerage once controlled only a small share of listings, but that changed in January when it acquired Anywhere Real Estate—the parent company of Coldwell Banker, Corcoran, Century 21 and Sotheby’s International Realty. According to some estimates, the mega-brokerage and its affiliates now handle more than 80% of Manhattan residential sales by dollar volume, as well as more than 30% of listings in other markets.

 

Compass says its model offers sellers more choice on how to market their homes, but critics say it is harming the consumer. Now the long-simmering industry dispute is spilling over into public view, with lawmakers and civil-rights advocates taking notice.

 

“[Pocket listings] were the exception,” said Bess Freedman, chief executive of Compass rival Brown Harris Stevens. “Compass is making them the rule.”

 
 
Compass CEO Robert Reffkin, shown in 2019, co-founded the company as Urban Compass in 2012. GO NAKAMURA FOR WSJ
 

How expensive is custom furniture? We talked to one homeowner who budgeted $60,000 to redo their kitchen, which felt cheap and dated. But after collaborating with a California-based designer on a custom redesign plan for the kitchen, dining area, an attached laundry room and entryway—which included all-new cabinetry, a bespoke banquette, slate floors and green soapstone counters—the cost swelled to roughly $180,000.

 

Rising labor costs, fluctuating tariffs, subsequent shipping delays and gridlock in the Strait of Hormuz have made custom furniture more expensive and difficult to procure. Prices have risen so sharply that even wealthy buyers are struggling to afford them.

 

In our latest series, we examined how four homeowners stayed on budget to build custom, architect-designed homes for under $1 million. Here’s what we learned.

 
 
 

The Fierce Battle to Control How Americans Buy and Sell Their Homes

 
 
FABIO CONSOLI FOR WSJ
 

Mega-brokerage Compass is taking more listings offline, sparking backlash from rivals who say the practice is upending decades of market transparency.

 
 
 
CONTENT FROM: WHITECAP
 
 
Whitecap: The New Watermark in Texas Coastal Living
 
The Texas Gulf Coast doesn't let go easily. At Whitecap, that pull becomes a place to put down roots. Now available on North Padre Island, a rare collection of homesites from the $300s unfolds across five miles of navigable canals, where private docks lead to open water and the landscape stretches into a 30-acre nature preserve.

Even Millionaires Can Barely Afford Custom Furniture These Days

 
 
CARA TOTMAN
 

Thanks to rising labor costs, President Trump’s tariffs and delayed shipping, custom pieces have ballooned in price and taken longer to arrive.

 
 
 

How to Build a Custom, Architect-Designed Home for Under $1 Million

 
 
JAKE PARRISH, THE WALL STREET JOURNAL
 

Smart, budget-conscious trade-offs helped the homeowners in our latest series lower construction costs without sacrificing design.

 
 
 

What’s the Deal?

 
 
CHRIS SNITKO/MODERN TAKE MEDIA
 

A contemporary Laguna Beach, Calif., home that cantilevers over the ocean has sold for $82.6 million, making it the second-highest sale recorded in affluent Orange County.

 

On the southwestern coast of Kauai, Hawaii, a roughly 5,000-square-foot estate that has been in the same family for more than 100 years is listing for $19.2 million.

 

Want to see more deals? Sign up for our Mansion Deals email alert to have the biggest and best luxury home sales and listings delivered to your inbox.

 
 
 

The Luxe Life

 
 
ABIGAIL JACKSON FOR WSJ
 

Two daughters from a blended family teamed up to design and build a 7,500-square-foot, four-bedroom house that leaned into their love of horses.

 

Michael Douglas remembers stepping out of his dad’s shadow after “Fatal Attraction” and “Wall Street.” “He said, ‘Michael, you’re a better actor than I ever was.’”

 
 
 

House of the Week

 
 
MONUMENT STUDIOS
 

WSJ’s latest House of the Week from Virginia Hunt Country looks like it’s been standing for centuries, though it was completed around 2005.

 

When subcontractors asked when he started the renovation, the owner would gleefully respond that it was actually a new house. “That is a very nice compliment,” he said, “because that’s what we were trying to accomplish.”

 
 
 

Your Home

 

• Many of the ingredients needed to cause a fall in U.S. home prices are in place, except for the one that really matters: owners who are desperate to sell.

 

• Home sales in September rose for the first time since May, with buyers taking advantage of a plateau in mortgage rates over the summer before the surge in recent weeks.

 

• A new type of mortgage—based on potential rental income, not the borrower’s wealth—is reviving long abandoned neighborhoods.
